body:
+1 to this! Bikeshedded specs use both "invoke"-style and "interest"-style popups, and the more declarative and accessible we can make those, the better.

In particular, I'm happy to see the events API in the explainer, which'll let me fill the popup on demand with the appropriate markup. A spec can easily have thousands of "interest" popups, and generating them all up-front (either in the static markup, or via JS on initialization) was a significant cost that I had to avoid by switching to purely on-demand DOM generation. It'll also simplify the interaction a bit, since I can just reuse a single popup element and won't have to uniquify IDs for all of them.

How does this work on mobile? There sometimes hover is simulated by a single tap and click is a subsequent tap.

Also, I somewhat doubt this can be truly input-agnostic as web developers are often quite particular about the kind of UX they want. It probably has to match to some extent across platforms as otherwise there would be no way to explain this to end users.

We have an open issue regarding touch inputs (https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1052). Right now we've resolved to make touch inputs implementation defined as there is a lack of cohesive UX across mobile platforms, but we're happy to define something if you think there is a tenable path to doing so.

The reason the mobile issue is relevant is b/c that affects whether this should have a name that's explicitly about hover, or a name like "interest" that suggests it is independent of input modality. 

On platforms where the primary pointer input is touch or gaze, there isn't an obvious good choice of "interest" user action.
* Touch: need to either not support "interest", or do "tap once for interest, twice to click", which is annoying and may not be what site authors want.
* Gaze (like the gaze-pinch system on Apple Vision Pro): gaze is an indicator of interest, but for privacy reasons can't expose any observable side effects to the page.
* XR Hand input: while in theory it's possible and not a privacy problem to to support hover as the user holding their hand near a point in a page but not quite touching it, that action is tiring and bad ergonomics.

Because of this, I think "hovertarget" is a better name than "interesttarget", because de facto it is tied to hover specifically, and does not actually represent an abstract idea independent of input modality.

Secondarily, it might be good to have advice on whether "interest" should be ignored or should get "simulated hover on first tap" behavior when using touch input, since it will make a big difference to authors which it is and they may affect how/whether they use this attribute. Other specs in the web platform explicitly or implicitly acknowledge the existence of touch input so I don't think it's wrong to address this case. Failing to do so is just biasing things towards platforms with mouse/trackpad input. We should not assume those are the norm and everything else is implementation defined IMO.
Fwiw this would also trigger for keyboard focus as currently proposed, so isn't just - hover on "desktop" platforms.

I think it's very worthwhile for folks to read the comments and discussion on https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/1052, since it's exactly about this question. The TL;DR opinion there is that for **keyboard** and **mouse**, the exact behaviors that define "showing interest" should be standardized. For other input modalities (touch, gaze, future-thing) the spec should say that UA's **must allow all users** to "show interest", while not specifically defining how to do it. The last thing is very important, or you get the problems that are the primary reason we need this API today: developers implement the behavior for the kinds of input modalities they have, and leave out users. E.g. most tooltips on the web today don't work very well for touch users. We'd like to use this API to fix that situation.

> Because of this, I think "hovertarget" is a better name than "interesttarget", because de facto it is tied to hover specifically, and does not actually represent an abstract idea independent of input modality.

As mentioned above, keyboard should be explicitly supported, which is why we didn't want to call it "hover". Also the stuff above, where all users should be able to show interest in something, not just those with a mouse or keyboard.

>  Other specs in the web platform explicitly or implicitly acknowledge the existence of touch input so I don't think it's wrong to address this case. Failing to do so is just biasing things towards platforms with mouse/trackpad input. We should not assume those are the norm and everything else is implementation defined IMO.

I think our preference would definitely be to standardize how to "show interest" using touch. But it's hard because that's a very platform and browser specific thing today. For example, Apple platforms previously had "force touch". Those have since moved on to "long press", but I'd guess it would have been unfortunate to standardize "showing interest" to be some length of long press, while ignoring what force touch users should be doing.

> The spec should say that UA's **must allow all users** to "show interest", while not specifically defining how to do it

How is Chromium planning to do this on Android?

> > The spec should say that UA's **must allow all users** to "show interest", while not specifically defining how to do it
> 
> How is Chromium planning to do this on Android?

Excellent question, and I don't think we've got a great answer yet. In my opinion, the best I've heard is to add an item to the top of the long-press context menu that can be used to "show interest". What it says is an open question, since "show interest" probably isn't a great explanation for most users for what that means/does. Another idea is to just not show the context menu if an item has `interesttarget`, and instead fire the interest event. I suspect that's likely a bad idea because it stops people from using the context menu on that item. Better ideas appreciated.

> We'd like to use this API to fix that situation.

I'm sorry, but I don't buy that this is going to fix the problem if we don't have a good story. You end up doing the exact same thing you blame web developers of. Also, web developers will want a particular experience. If the experience is going to be inconsistent or non-existent it's not going to be a feature they can adopt.

> > We'd like to use this API to fix that situation.
> 
> I'm sorry, but I don't buy that this is going to fix the problem if we don't have a good story. You end up doing the exact same thing you blame web developers of. Also, web developers will want a particular experience. If the experience is going to be inconsistent or non-existent it's not going to be a feature they can adopt.

Help me understand your comment. Are you saying you'd like to add specific details to the standard for all input modalities? E.g. force touch and eye tracking and whatnot? Or perhaps just writing down the details for mobile/touchscreen and leaving eye tracking out? Are you saying the "interest based triggering" use case isn't valid? Are you saying something else?

I think there are a few key differences between all developers everywhere re-implementing interest-based triggering, and three browser engines implementing it once for everyone. There's clear value in the latter, because everyone gets the benefit. If one browser or platform is missing support for interest triggering, bugs will be filed and hopefully fixed.

As to inconsistency between platforms, that's baked in today. If a developer wants to build a tooltip, they **can't** address eye tracking users, full stop. They *often* leave out keyboard users, and very often leave out touch users. On the other hand, with the `interesttarget` attribute, they would be able to declaratively say what they want, and rely on browsers to allow their users to access that functionality, regardless of input modality.

Would WebKit be supportive of defining "showing interest" on mobile/touch platforms to be done via long-press? I.e. the spec would say that a long-press (defined somehow) is the exact mechanism for showing interest. That would preclude showing any context menus on long-press for those elements wearing `interesttarget`, and it would preclude using other mechanisms such as 3D touch (iOS), touch-based-hover built in to the OS (Android), stylus hover mechanisms, etc. to "show interest".

I think that would at least solve your comment for touchscreens. I'm not sure what to propose for eye tracking or other novel interfaces. If there's a standard/universal way to describe a Vision Pro gesture that "shows interest", I suppose we could see about adding it to the spec also?

It's a pretty common pattern on Android native apps to have "interest" like information behind a long press, avoiding cases where that long press also triggers a context menu. E.g.

Long press on + button in system Clock app:
![Screenshot_20240603_125007_Clock](https://github.com/whatwg/html/assets/366761/f2eb2faf-caa9-4494-aed3-d72be3225a10)

Long press on magnifying glass in Android Settings:
![Screenshot_20240603_125113_Settings](https://github.com/whatwg/html/assets/366761/45d50499-6df0-439b-b2f0-a0728306df53)

Long press on lightning icon in Android camera app:
![Screenshot_20240603_125220_Camera](https://github.com/whatwg/html/assets/366761/8e0c0a74-3385-432b-a813-a6a32305671e)

I don't see any reason interest on the web couldn't follow the same pattern. Currently on Android web, only images and links have a default context menu. There's also precedent for adding a shorter timeout to one action over the other. E.g. user long presses, after 300ms it no longer produces a click and the interest is triggered, after 500ms a contextmenu is triggered. Drag and drop on the iOS home screen exhibits this: after a short press the item is picked up for dragging, after a long press the context menu is shown.

It's also worth noting that pressing and holding can already trigger `:hover` behaviors (without clicking) as the web already has established this for compat reasons: https://jsbin.com/gesupif/edit?html,css,js,output

> There's also precedent for adding a shorter timeout to one action over the other. E.g. user long presses, after 300ms it no longer produces a click and the interest is triggered, after 500ms a contextmenu is triggered. Drag and drop on the iOS home screen exhibits this: after a short press the item is picked up for dragging, after a long press the context menu is shown.

I wonder whether users can navigate this well - it sounds like they have a 200ms window of time to get the "interest" behavior? This is why I was leaning towards including "interest" in the context menu, so that there's only one delay and users have easy access to both things from one menu. I could also see *only* showing the "interest" and never showing the context menu, but I'm guessing that'll lead to frustration sometimes.

> It's also worth noting that pressing and holding can already trigger `:hover` behaviors (without clicking) as the web already has established this for compat reasons: https://jsbin.com/gesupif/edit?html,css,js,output

This is true. But I'd like to avoid the "double-menu" situation for interest invokers, since I know that causes user frustration in other contexts at least, such as autocomplete. Here's what I see on iOS:

![IMG_9202](https://github.com/whatwg/html/assets/29559695/cfd19686-0891-429c-b9df-910be807f111)

> user long presses, after 300ms it no longer produces a click and the interest is triggered, after 500ms a contextmenu is triggered

I do like this idea. Although, it may be an issue for users with mobility issues, as it requires them to hold down for longer to get the context menu.

Also, most users are already familair with holding down for a certain amount of time for a context menu to appear, so this could break their consistency. This would also make them uncertain on what to expect with every link.

And an interest target might appear over the link, so the user can't long press to view the context menu.

---

> But I'd like to avoid the "double-menu" situation for interest invokers

On Android Chrome and Firefox, at least, both links and buttons' text cannot be direcly selected, they only can be selected when text around them is selected and then dragged over. Does iOS also do this?

> On Android Chrome and Firefox, at least, both links and buttons' text cannot be direcly selected, they only can be selected when text around them is selected and then dragged over. Does iOS also do this?

On iOS Safari, button text is selectable. (See the screenshot above.) Links are not selectable, and they have a separate "full screen link preview" that shows up if you long-press. That would obviously have to go away or be modified, in the case that the `<a>` had an `interesttarget` attribute attached, since the current behavior takes over the screen and would cover any popover launched by the `interesttarget`.

> And an interest target might appear over the link, so the user can't long press to view the context menu.

The context menu would still target to the original element. Touch has [implicit capture](https://www.w3.org/TR/pointerevents/#implicit-pointer-capture) resulting in all subsequent events targeting the original element (i.e. before the interest target popped up).

I happened to be reading the [spec for close requests](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#close-requests) today, which says:

> In an [implementation-defined](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#implementation-defined) (and likely device-specific) manner, a user can send a close request to the user agent. This indicates that the user wishes to close something that is currently being shown on the screen, such as a popover, menu, dialog, picker, or display mode.
> 
> Some example close requests are:
> 
> The Esc key on desktop platforms.
> 
> The back button or gesture on certain mobile platforms such as Android.
> 
> Any assistive technology's dismiss gesture, such as iOS VoiceOver's two-finger scrub "z" gesture.
> 
> A game controller's canonical "back" button, such as the circle button on a DualShock gamepad.

That seems like a great way to spec something that is very device-specific and needs to be open-ended to allow for innovation on the UI surfaces of devices. My proposal for `interesttarget` would be to use very similar language, including the non-normative examples list, but with the one change from "a user **can** send..." to something like "a user **must be able to** send...".

A quick update on this issue. After *much* discussion and work in OpenUI, [the explainer](https://open-ui.org/components/interest-invokers.explainer/) has been significantly updated. While there is still work to be done, we believe we've found great solutions to the issues posed above, relating to the need for a *specific* method for "showing interest" via a touchscreen interface. In particular, this section of the explainer covers touchscreen activation in detail:

- https://open-ui.org/components/interest-invokers.explainer/#touchscreen

The TL;DR is:
1. When an element such as a link has `interesttarget`, long-pressing that element will **both** trigger interest (e.g. show a popover) **and** show the existing context menu.
2. In this case, the context menu will not blur its background (as it often does on browsers today) and will position itself such that ~half of the viewport is still uncovered by the menu.
3. New [env() values](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/env) will expose the "safe" area of the viewport in which to position a popover.
4. Tapping the popover dismisses the context menu, and tapping the context menu triggers a loss of interest in the `interesttarget` element (typically hiding the popover).

The net result, which seems to make developers quite happy, is that **a)** long-press is the (very familiar) activation method, and **b)** the user still has ready access to both the hovercard/popover and the context menu.

Comments, suggestions, and improvements are very much appreciated.
This sounds very good to me!

Agenda+ to propose moving this to [Stage 1](https://whatwg.org/stages#stage1):
- A comprehensive [explainer](https://open-ui.org/components/interest-invokers.explainer/).
- Consensus that the WHATWG is interested in exploring solutions in this problem space: to be discussed.
- One implementer interested in doing prototyping work: Chromium.
- Identification of the Contributor: me.
- Identification of a relevant WHATWG Workstream and Standard: WHATWG/html and CSSWG.
I've prepared a [draft PR](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11006) for this feature, and dropped some questions on the nitty gritty in there.
Per the [last WHATNOT meeting](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11010), this is now at stage 1.

Quick update here, for those not involved in the other active discussions of this feature. I've updated the [explainer](https://open-ui.org/components/interest-invokers.explainer) significantly. For those interested, you can check out:

- Expanded [web survey data](https://open-ui.org/components/interest-invokers.explainer/#the-pitch) showing that 94+% of production web sites use hover-triggered UI today.
- Additional data that 9/10 native apps use long-press as the UX pattern for "showing interest" in something.
- A [detailed survey](https://open-ui.org/components/interest-invokers.explainer/#survey-of-use-cases) of specific sites using hover-triggering, categorized into use cases (Page preview, Tooltips, More info, Quick actions, Hover menus).
- An [analysis](https://open-ui.org/components/interest-invokers.explainer/#survey-conclusions) of those same sites, showing whether/how they support keyboard and touch activation. Short story: not great.
- A [greatly expanded touchscreen section](https://open-ui.org/components/interest-invokers.explainer/#touchscreen) that enumerates all of the proposed options for touchscreen support, each with helpful mockups of what the behavior would look like for links and buttons. (Our current preference is option 3 - add an item to the context menu.)
- Some additional tweaks and cleanups.

I'd love it if folks could give it a look and let me know your thoughts. We are also working to gather developer feedback on the overall feature, as well as the various touchscreen options, and I'll include that data in the explainer when it's available.

Hi, I discovered this topic thanks to @una's talk at Google I/O.
I'm a cross-platform developer and have encountered this type of scenario in my (React-)Native iOS/iPadOS/Android app and its twin PWA.  

TL;DR: I don’t think that hovering with a mouse represents the same interest or level of user engagement as a long press on a touchscreen.

## Mobile First

  All the reflection on how to bring content from desktop/mouse environments to mobile/touchscreen devices—where these patterns don't naturally exist—is very useful. The use cases listed for the different types of hovercards are also very interesting, and some of them align well with the long-press scenario on touchscreens, such as **page previews**.

  But if you start the reflection from the mobile/touchscreen perspective (mobile-first design) and consider the long-press interaction, I don't think that hover is the true counterpart to long press.

  The long-press interaction on touchscreens is commonly used in native apps, but it doesn't offer the same level of discoverability as hover. In fact, long press tends to function more like a _shortcut_ for "power users".
Any interaction accessible via long press should still be possible without it.

For example, in a list of items, you might long-press an item to reveal quick actions—but those same actions should also be accessible elsewhere, like on the item’s detail screen, after tapping on it.

### List Items Screen

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7b4b0010-0713-4e8f-88ad-7515a797665e)

### Item Screen

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/669f98b1-90ca-43bd-a210-0f981e831386)

## Right click

In my opinion, the true **counterpart to the long-press interaction is the right-click** on desktop.
All the detailed options for handling long-press scenarios on touchscreens (Option 1 - leave the details to UA / Option 2 - show both at the same time / Option 3 - add an item to the context menu / etc.) closely mirror the kinds of challenges and design considerations we face when implementing right-click interactions in desktop web apps.

## Button size

Also, in the hovercard scenario on desktop or mouse-based devices, the button or link that triggers the hovercard is usually small—like a short piece of text or a round icon. But on touchscreen devices, the trigger for a long-press interaction is often much larger—usually the entire item itself.  

### Small Screen

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a37b3950-1b22-4ecc-bcf1-dabd0e22421e)

### Larger Screen

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8800f0ed-c0da-4849-9a75-93fa77cc4d95)

So, if we want to implement long-press **quick actions** on a list of items for mobile/touchscreen using `interesttarget`, that would mean the entire list item becomes a hover target on desktop/mouse—which would trigger the `popover`! Even with a long delay on hover, this could be really annoying and distracting for users.  

---

I hope I’ve explained my point of view: that long press on touchscreens isn’t the right counterpart for all types of mouse hover interactions.  

But I think the concept of "interest" is interesting because:
* Some touchscreens can actually trigger hover, like tablets with a stylus, for example.
* XR devices with eye tracking also seem to use hover effects. However, in the case of visionOS, on Safari, you can’t style CSS hover or access hover events with JavaScript for privacy reasons. So having an intent-based interaction that lets developers open hovercards without JavaScript could be useful, but if we can’t even style hover with CSS, I’m not sure if user agents will implement it anytime soon.
* For now, in my opinion, there’s no way to replicate the same intent on touchscreens as hover with a mouse. But maybe in the future, with eye tracking on mobile devices, that could change. For now, interactions on touchscreens will differ from desktop/mouse hovercards use cases.


 Also, I think exploring the long-press interaction on the web is valuable, especially when considering it alongside **mouse right-click** scenarios. It would be very useful to have native app-like interactions that work smoothly and naturally in the browser.  

Thank you.

> TL;DR: I don’t think that hovering with a mouse represents the same interest or level of user engagement as a long press on a touchscreen.

Thanks for your detailed analysis of the situation. I just want to confirm one thing: you essentially support a new "option 7" which is **"do not support touchscreen users for `interesttarget`"**. Is that correct? (Other than those with a stylus or other "hover-capable" feature.) If so, I can add such an option to the explainer.

Yes, I believe my opinion represents, as you said, a new 'Option 7: Do not support touchscreen users for `interesttarget`.'

edit : I tried to summarize my understanding of the use cases and corresponding interactions on a touchscreen.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dac97f9d-3ac7-4748-95a4-7f527724e298)

I'm interested in these for implementing footnotes (hovernotes?). These would often be short, but could be quite long and contain footnotes themselves (including fully general footnote digraphs), and can definitely contain links. Think David Foster Wallace or *House of Leaves* or, less extremely, Terry Pratchett or Wikipedia. I have a bunch of context from implementing these the present hard way (i.e., with mouseenter/mouseleave, open-coding waits, etc) still paged in, so I'll go down a bunch of considerations and thoughts on the proposal. Broadly, I like the idea of interest invokers very much, but there are several fiddly details to be filled in, including some potential dealbreakers.

In my present implementation, what's shown on hover is the same as what's shown on click, with the difference being that hovering away will close what was opened only by hover, while click-opened popovers stick around until they're actively dismissed somehow, so short footnotes can be cheaply opened, glanced at and cheaply dismissed, while long footnotes can be persisted so they're not accidentally closed and you have to re-open and find your place again, possibly several footnotes deep. Another benefit is that if there isn't sufficiently-fine mouse control to keep a goes-away-on-unhover popover open, the footnotes are still easily accessible.

For this UI pattern, I wouldn't at all mind if interest wasn't wired up at all on touchscreens, since the hover behaviour is only a convenience for mouse users to save a click to open and a click to close, and e.g. long pressing or tapping twice to access what's available with one short tap is a bit silly; if those options are present (presumably to serve other interest invoker use-cases), it doesn't really hurt except for possibly mildly confusing users about what the point of them is.

With similar reasoning, I also decided not to show a footnote on focus but rather to wait for activation so that tabbing through the page isn't annoying with having to repeatedly close each footnote as you come to it, but, if interest invokers become a standard bit of the Web UI toolbox, I'd be happy doing whatever the platform decides to do as the thing that's least surprising. I do wonder in this sort of case, where `interesttarget` and `invoketarget` are doing the same thing, if there shouldn't be some way to suppress interest invocation, but then I start wondering whether authors would inappropriately use it where some things are only available through interest invocation... Perhaps the case where the `interesttarget` and the `invoketarget` are the same could be special-cased, but I'm not sure there aren't similar cases where they won't be identical but still wind up subsumed. And of course authors can just not use `interesttarget` but open-code if they _really_ want one behaviour or the other.

When a popover is closed, focus will often then land on the popover's invoker (see openui/open-ui#327)... which, if interest-on-focus, then causes interest in the popover again and it's re-opened. Maybe this sort of automatic movement on focus oughtn't trigger interest, but then I can see users getting confused about why focus is on an element but interest isn't being shown as it normally would.

The general idea of recursive popovers and interest-triggered display suggests a rule that showing interest in a descendant popover should retain interest in its ancestors; interest being lost in an ancestor should close its descendants, but that ought to come for free.

It'd be weird for losing interest like hovering away can close popovers that were opened by heavier action like a click on the trigger, which would defeat my goal of letting users persist footnotes so they're not accidentally closed. I'd prefer something more like a tristate: closed, interest-shown, and explicitly-opened; losing interest in the interest-shown state would close the popover, but only an active dismissal can close it from the explicitly-opened state. There are some knock-on considerations:
  - Clicking on the trigger button in an interest-shown popover should definitely promote to explicitly-opened (and then another click should toggle back to closed, if it is indeed a toggle), and the popover shouldn't be closed as part of this interaction.
  - I treat clicking on an interest-shown popover as promoting it to explicitly-opened, but I haven't thought deeply about whether that's good universal behaviour. Some thought probably needs to be given to interacting with controls or links inside the popover and whether that should promote.
  - I don't know if it makes sense to have an explicitly-opened popover be a descendant of a merely interest-shown popover; ancestor popovers probably need to be promoted when a descendant is if that promotion isn't to be pointless.
  - There should be an event fired at promotion for user code to listen to to e.g. adjust styling if explicitly-opened popovers are distinguished from the merely interest-shown. It should be distinguishable from a direct closed to explicitly-opened transition (because, e.g., the popover could be dynamically filled and that was already done when it shown before vs needing to be done as it's opened the first time).
  - Can you have interest-shown popovers 'in parallel' to explicitly-opened ones (i.e., where the popovers do not form a single stack, but rather has a branching point)? If not, then there's a hazard of having an explicitly-opened popover somewhere offscreen preventing interest being shown in another one, which could be confusing for users.

I definitely want interest-shown popovers to be explicitly dismissable, which likely means hooking in with close watchers. Because interest-shown popovers are so light and not triggered by something that counts as user activation, there's an issue with close watchers' anti-trapping behaviour: repeatedly hovering a trigger button and then pressing Escape leads to divergent results, sometimes only closing the interest-shown popover and sometimes closing other things on the page (when the anti-trapping behaviour triggers). I've convinced myself a solution would be to have a variant of close watchers that doesn't intercept and consume the close request, but rather fires its event when a close request is received and then passes it down to the next layer (which might be another close watcher and closes something else on the page, or, if there aren't any, it might be the browser navigating back (like Android's back gesture), or it might just do nothing (like pressing Escape)); these would be for closing things triggered by similarly light interactions as showing interest that don't count as user activation, and which wouldn't need to care about anti-trapping because the layer below also gets the close request.

Another problem with close requests and interest invocation will be race conditions. The mechanism above would also solve these by making it predictable that the topmost popover (or whatever) opened by deliberate user action will always be closed, as well as any interest-shown popovers, no matter whether the interest-lost event wins or loses the race against the close request.

> Broadly, I like the idea of interest invokers very much, but there are several fiddly details to be filled in, including some potential dealbreakers.

Thanks for the detail notes/feedback!

> In my present implementation, what's shown on hover is the same as what's shown on click, with the difference being that hovering away will close what was opened only by hover, while click-opened popovers stick around until they're actively dismissed somehow...

This is a great use case. And I agree with the approach it sounds like you've taken, of using both `interestfor` and `commandfor` on the same element. They should play nicely together, so any issues you encounter will be important to fix. 

> For this UI pattern, I wouldn't at all mind if interest wasn't wired up at all on touchscreens, since the hover behaviour is only a convenience for mouse users to save a click to open and a click to close, and e.g. long pressing or tapping twice to access what's available with one short tap is a bit silly; if those options are present (presumably to serve other interest invoker use-cases), it doesn't really hurt except for possibly mildly confusing users about what the point of them is.

I'm a little loathe to add special behaviors (e.g. not implementing part of the `interestfor` behavior when `commandfor` is present, since a) it's a special case, and b) we'll have to be very careful that the `interestfor` and `commandfor` behavior are the same. E.g. they'd both have to point at the same element, have the same behavior (`command=toggle-popover`), and probably some other checks. I feel like it's probably safer to have both attributes just always do their normal thing, even when used together.


> I do wonder in this sort of case, where `interesttarget` and `invoketarget` are doing the same thing, if there shouldn't be some way to suppress interest invocation, but then I start wondering whether authors would inappropriately use it where some things are only available through interest invocation... Perhaps the case where the `interesttarget` and the `invoketarget` are the same could be special-cased, but I'm not sure there aren't similar cases where they won't be identical but still wind up subsumed. And of course authors can just not use `interesttarget` but open-code if they _really_ want one behaviour or the other.

Exactly! I agree.


> When a popover is closed, focus will often then land on the popover's invoker (see [openui/open-ui#327](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/327))... which, if interest-on-focus, then causes interest in the popover again and it's re-opened. This one is interesting, and if true, should be fixed. The "return focus to the invoker" behavior shouldn't trigger interest again.
